dailyTips: Memorise squares up to 25 and cubes up to 10. Recognising 289 as 17 squared or 729 as 9 cubed saves seconds on every roots and exponents question.
For percent problems, pick 100 as the starting value. It turns abstract percent changes into plain arithmetic you can do in your head.
Percent change always divides by the original value. If a price goes from 80 to 100, that's 20 out of 80, so 25 percent, not 20 percent.
Average speed over a round trip is total distance over total time. It is never just the average of the two speeds unless the times are equal.
When a problem says 'remainder 3 when divided by 5', write the number as 5k + 3 and test k = 0, 1, 2. It makes the pattern obvious.
Test numbers in Yes/No questions with variables: try 0, 1, a negative, and a fraction. Most traps hide in those four.
Before dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, ask if it could be zero. If so, factor instead and keep that root.
Factor first, expand never, unless the question makes you. Expressions like x² − 9 become (x − 3)(x + 3) and often cancel neatly.
To compare fractions, cross-multiply or convert to decimals using known values like 1/8 = 0.125. Don't find common denominators when a benchmark works.
For 'x is what percent of y', write x/y and multiply by 100. The word after 'of' goes on the bottom.
If a quantity is multiplied by 1.2 and then 0.8, the result is 0.96, not 1. Successive percent changes multiply; they don't add.
Combined work: add rates, not times. If one person takes 6 hours and another takes 3, their combined rate is 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so 2 hours.
Count the units on a rate problem. Minutes versus hours is the most common slip, so convert everything first.
Factorials cancel. For 10!/8! just compute 10 × 9. Never multiply out the big numbers.
For the number of factors, write the prime factorisation, add 1 to each exponent and multiply. 72 = 2³ × 3² gives 4 × 3 = 12 factors.
The units digit of powers repeats in cycles. For 2, 3, 7 and 8 the cycle is 4, so divide the exponent by 4 and look at the remainder.
When you add the same constant to every number in a set, the standard deviation stays the same. Only multiplying changes it.
On weighted average problems, the answer lies between the two group averages and nearer the bigger group. Use that to eliminate choices.
For overlapping sets, a two-by-two table is safer than a Venn diagram when the problem has 'neither' or percentages.
Combinations: choose 2 from 7 is 7 × 6 / 2 = 21. Write the numerator and denominator first, then cancel, rather than expanding factorials.
'At least one' probability is almost always 1 minus the chance of none. It turns a long case count into one line.
Backsolve when the answers are clean numbers and the question asks for one value. Start with choice C and move up or down based on the result.
Estimate first when answer choices are far apart. Rounding 49 to 50 or 3.9 to 4 can eliminate three options in ten seconds.
When you read a word problem, write what is being asked at the top of your scratch paper. It stops you answering the wrong question.
For inequalities, never multiply or divide by a negative without flipping the sign. If the sign of the variable is unknown, move terms and factor instead.
Absolute value equations split into two cases. |x − 3| = 5 means x − 3 = 5 or x − 3 = −5, so x = 8 or x = −2.
Don't solve what you don't have to. If the question asks for x + y, look for a way to get x + y directly before solving each separately.
Know the difference between 'percent of' and 'percent more than'. 150 is 150 percent of 100, and also 50 percent more than 100.
Know the difference between 'per cent more than' and 'per cent of'. 150 is 150 percent of 100 and also 50 percent more than 100.
Evenly spaced sets have mean equal to median. Their sum is the count times the middle value, which is usually the fastest way to add a long list.
Quant has no calculator, so the numbers are built to be friendly. If your arithmetic gets ugly, you've probably taken a wrong turn.
For a ratio problem, introduce a multiplier k. A 3:5 ratio becomes 3k and 5k, and the problem becomes ordinary algebra.
A quadratic with a positive product of roots and a negative sum has two negative roots. Check signs before solving, especially in Data Sufficiency.
Perfect squares have an odd number of factors. It's a neat fact that the GMAT likes to hide inside number properties questions.
Remember that 1 is neither prime nor composite and 0 is even. These edge cases appear in 'must be true' questions.
For 'must be true' number property questions, try to find one case that breaks each choice. One counterexample kills an answer.
Use the 'divide by a common factor' shortcut for ratios and fractions before turning to decimals. It keeps arithmetic exact.
Compound interest grows faster than simple interest only after the first period. After one year they are equal.
Read Data Sufficiency stems twice, then rephrase them. 'Is x > y?' is the same as 'Is x − y positive?' and that clue guides the statements.
When two Data Sufficiency statements give two equations, check that they are truly independent. Doubling an equation doesn't add information.
On Quant, anything over about two and a half minutes without clear progress is a signal to guess and move on.
Slow down on the first few questions of each section. The adaptive test builds its view of you from them, so accuracy early matters.
If you spot an easy question, don't get suspicious and overthink. Easy questions exist even at high levels.
Practise mental maths daily for five minutes. Fluency with multiplication, squares and fractions buys you whole minutes per section.
After every practice set, list each wrong answer as concept, careless or timing. The fix is different for each, and you'll see your pattern fast.
Redo questions you got wrong after three days without looking at the solution. If you can't, the concept hasn't sunk in yet.
Spaced practice beats cramming. Twenty minutes a day for six days outperforms one two-hour block, especially for formulas and vocabulary.
Write neatly on your scratch pad. Cramped, messy working is the number one cause of careless errors under time pressure.
Always check the target of the question one last time before you click. Many wrong answers are correct solutions to the wrong question.
On Quant word problems, define variables clearly with units, like 'x = number of apples'. It prevents mixing up quantities mid-solution.
In Critical Reasoning, read the question stem before the passage. Knowing whether you're strengthening, weakening or finding an assumption tells you what to look for.
Find the conclusion first, then the evidence. Look for words like 'therefore', 'so', and 'thus' for conclusions, and 'because' or 'since' for premises.
The assumption is the gap between the evidence and the conclusion. Ask yourself: what must be true for these premises to lead there?
Use the negation test on an assumption answer: if denying it destroys the argument, it is necessary. Use it to check, not to hunt.
To weaken a causal argument, think of three things: another cause, reversed cause and effect, or pure coincidence. Most weaken answers are one of these.
To strengthen a causal argument, rule out other causes or show the effect disappears when the cause does.
In weaken questions, don't aim to disprove. The right answer only has to make the conclusion less likely, even slightly.
Wrong answers in CR love to be 'out of scope'. If an option introduces a new idea the argument never touches, it's almost always wrong.
For inference questions, choose the answer that must be true, not the one that could be. It should feel boring and cautious.
Be suspicious of extreme words in Verbal answers: always, never, all, only, completely. The GMAT usually rewards the moderate choice.
In paradox questions, the correct answer explains how both facts can be true. An answer that denies one of the facts is wrong.
In boldface questions, label each bold statement as premise, conclusion, objection or background before you look at the choices.
For 'evaluate the argument' questions, ask whether the answer to the choice's question could swing the conclusion either way. If both answers help, it's the one.
Reading Comprehension is a map-reading task. Note the purpose of each paragraph in a few words, not every detail.
Underline the contrast words in RC: however, but, although, yet. The author's real view often follows them.
In RC detail questions, always go back and find the sentence. Never trust memory, as wrong answers are designed to feel familiar.
Pay attention to the author's tone words: adjectives and adverbs like 'unfortunately', 'merely' and 'remarkably' reveal attitude.
For a main idea question, check that your answer covers the whole passage. If it only fits one paragraph, it's too narrow.
In RC inference questions, the right answer is usually one small logical step from the passage, not a leap.
Don't use outside knowledge on RC or CR. If you know the topic well, resist the urge to bring facts the passage didn't give.
When you're down to two answers in CR, compare them directly: which one connects the premise to the conclusion more tightly?
Prephrase before you read the options. Even a rough idea of the right answer protects you from attractive wrong ones.
On RC, spend about a minute and a half reading a short passage and two minutes on a longer one. Over-reading steals time from questions.
Match answer choices to the passage by meaning, not by matching words. Answers that copy phrases word for word are often traps.
Learn the families of CR flaws: causal, sampling, analogy, necessary vs sufficient and part vs whole. Naming the flaw speeds you up.
In a CR stimulus, a plan or prediction always has an assumption that nothing will interfere. Weaken answers often show something that does.
Keep a running list of vocabulary that trips you up in passages, like 'tenuous' or 'ostensibly'. Review it for five minutes a week.
When a CR argument compares two groups, ask whether the groups are really comparable. Many weaken answers point out an important difference.
If a CR question uses the words 'most strongly supports', treat it as an inference question, not a strengthen question. Read the stem carefully.
Statistics in CR are a trap. Percentages without actual numbers can hide a small base, and numbers without percentages can hide a large one.
For 'logically completes' questions, predict the next sentence from the direction of the argument. Signal words like 'but' or 'so' point the way.
On RC, distinguish what the author says from what other people in the passage say. Questions often test whose view it is.
Read the first and last sentences of each RC paragraph carefully. They often carry the structure of the passage.
If an RC passage feels dense, paraphrase each paragraph in plain words as you go. Understanding beats speed on the first read.
In CR, a correct answer to a weaken question could be false in real life and still be right. The question says 'if true', so take each option as fact.
For tone questions, compare strength: 'critical' and 'hostile' are different. Choose the word that matches the author's intensity.
Eliminate two quickly, then decide between the remaining pair. Don't waste time re-reading all five choices from scratch.
For application questions in RC, find the principle behind the passage, then choose the new case that follows the same pattern.
Data Insights starts with reading the title, axis labels and units. Many errors come from misreading thousands versus millions.
In Data Sufficiency, evaluate each statement separately before combining them. Mixing statements early is how people fall into the C trap.
Use the AD/BCE grid in Data Sufficiency: if statement 1 is sufficient, the answer is A or D; if not, it's B, C or E.
A definite 'No' is sufficient in a Yes/No Data Sufficiency question. People forget this and mark 'insufficient' when the answer is always no.
In Data Sufficiency, you don't need to solve. Once you're sure a statement gives one answer, stop and move on.
Rephrase Data Sufficiency questions before reading statements. 'What is the average?' often means 'what are the sum and the count?'
In Table Analysis, sort by the column the statement mentions. A sorted table makes top, bottom and median questions quick.
In Table Analysis, pay attention to boundaries like 'at least' and 'more than'. Check the exact cell values at the cut-off.
In Graphics Interpretation, read the sentence before looking at the graph in detail, so you know exactly what to extract.
In Two-Part Analysis, the two parts depend on each other. Write the constraints first, then test choices in pairs.
In Multi-Source Reasoning, skim every tab's structure, then read the question, then go back for just the facts you need.
The on-screen calculator exists only in Data Insights. Use it for messy multiplication and division, but estimate first so a typing slip is obvious.
In Data Insights, check whether a chart shows percentages or absolute numbers. A bigger percent of a smaller base can be a smaller amount.
A bar chart that doesn't start at zero exaggerates differences. Read the numbers, not the length of the bars.
Scatter plots show association, not cause. Pick answers that say 'is associated with' unless the passage gives a reason to claim more.
When a Data Insights question gives you a table and a chart together, check that the units and years match before combining numbers.
In Data Insights, round numbers to make mental maths easy, but only when the answer options are far enough apart to allow it.
In Data Sufficiency, if a statement gives a quadratic, look for two roots. Unless something rules one out, that statement is insufficient.
Stuck on a Data Insights question after two minutes? Make your best guess, bookmark it and move on. Another question is worth the same.
Don't memorise Data Insights formats. Practise reading structure: what is being asked, what is given, and what is the shortest route between them.
Time yourself on each Data Insights type separately. Table Analysis and Graphics Interpretation can often be done quicker than Multi-Source sets.
Aim for about two minutes per question on average. That means some questions take one minute and others three, so budget accordingly.
Use the first pass in Review & Edit wisely: bookmark questions where you are genuinely unsure, not every question that felt hard.
You can change only three answers per section in Review & Edit. Keep those for questions where you now see a clear, specific error.
Never leave a question blank. A guess has a chance of being right, and unanswered questions carry a penalty.
Choose your section order during practice, not on test day. Try two or three orders in your mocks and pick the one where you feel sharpest.
Keep an error log with three columns: what happened, why, and what to do next time. Review it every Sunday for ten minutes.
Mix topics in practice once you've learned the basics. The real exam doesn't announce the topic, so you have to recognise it yourself.
Take a full mock under exam conditions at least a few times. Stamina is a skill, and two hours of concentration needs training.
Review a mock for longer than it took to sit. Look for patterns in timing, question types and the mistakes you made repeatedly.
Practise guessing strategically. Eliminate even one or two options when stuck, then pick: two eliminated gives you a one-in-three shot, far better than a blank.
Study in short, focused blocks. Twenty-five minutes of full attention followed by a five-minute break beats an hour on autopilot.
Do your hardest topic when you're freshest. Save flashcards and review for low-energy hours, like the metro commute.
Use flashcards on your phone during idle moments: waiting for chai, standing in a queue. Five minutes a day adds up.
Say your reasoning out loud as you solve a problem. If you can't explain a step simply, you probably haven't understood it yet.
Teach a concept to someone, or to the wall. Explaining it in your own words is the fastest way to find the holes.
Before the exam, plan your test-day routine: sleep, breakfast, ID, travel time. The fewer decisions you make that morning, the better.
Check the ID rules early. In India you need a valid original passport at the test centre, so confirm yours is current well before exam day.
Plan your retake window now, even if you hope not to need it. Knowing there's a safety net lowers pressure on the first attempt.
Take a break only if you need one. If you do, use the ten minutes to eat, stretch and reset, and don't review questions.
Reduce study in the last three days. Light review and good sleep beat a last-minute cram that leaves you tired on test day.
Sleep is study time. Memory consolidates overnight, so a good night after a session locks in what you learned.
Track your accuracy by topic, not just overall score. A flat total can hide a topic that has quietly improved or slipped.
Don't compare your day thirty to someone else's day three hundred. Compare yourself to last week, and keep the line moving up.
A wrong answer you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed. Always find out why before moving on.
Fix one weakness at a time. Trying to repair everything at once tends to fix nothing.
Plan your week on Sunday: which days are long sessions, which are short ones, and which are rest. A plan removes daily decisions.
Tie your study to a cue, like right after your evening chai. Habits stick better when they follow something you already do.
Don't skip the 'why' in solutions. The GMAT recycles patterns, so understanding the reasoning helps you on questions you've never seen.
If you are scoring well in one section and badly in another, shift time toward the weak one, but don't abandon the strong one completely.
Your first mock score is a baseline, not a prediction. Most learners improve a lot between the first mock and the last.
Protect your confidence. When you've had a rough session, redo a few easy questions to end on a win.
Perfection is not the goal. Even high scorers miss questions. Aim for consistent accuracy and good time management.
Treat nervous energy as useful. A little adrenaline sharpens focus; slow breathing and a steady pace keep it from taking over.
On test day, if one question shakes you, let it go. Take a breath, reset, and treat the next question as a fresh start.
Remember why you're doing this. Pin your target school or career goal where you will see it when motivation dips.
Celebrate small wins: a finished lesson, a streak, a topic cleared. Progress that you notice is progress you keep.
Don't aim to feel ready; aim to be consistent. Readiness follows repetition, not the other way round.
When you hit a plateau, change the method rather than the amount. Try new question types, timed sets or teaching the idea aloud.
The GMAT tests judgement as much as knowledge. Practise deciding quickly what is worth solving and what is worth skipping.
If you feel overwhelmed, shrink the task. One flashcard deck, one lesson, one set. Starting small still counts as starting.
Keep your phone on silent in study blocks. Every notification costs you far more time than the few seconds it takes to glance.
motivation: You don't need to be a maths person. You need to be a practice person, and that part is entirely in your hands.
Every GMAT high scorer once got a percent problem wrong. The difference is they kept going.
Progress is rarely a straight line. A dip on Tuesday is just noise in a rising trend.
You have a full-time job, a life, and a goal. Studying on top of that is hard, and you're doing it. That counts.
Think of each session as a deposit. Small amounts, regularly made, add up to something big by August 2027.
You have about ten months to go. That isn't pressure; it's a gift. Use it patiently.
The GMAT tests reasoning, and you reason every day at work. You're not starting from zero.
A hard question doesn't mean you're failing. It means the test thinks you can handle more.
Confidence is built from evidence. Each practice set you finish is another piece of proof.
Your marketing background is an asset. You already read data, spot weak arguments, and explain ideas clearly. Bring that.
Slow is fine. Skipped is not. Show up even for ten minutes.
No one in a good business school got there by being perfect. They got there by being persistent.
Don't measure today against your goal. Measure it against yesterday.
If it feels hard, you're learning. If it feels easy, you're reviewing. Both are useful.
You can't control the questions on exam day. You can control how prepared you are, and you are working on that.
Treat the GMAT like cricket practice, not a one-day miracle: nets every day, and match day takes care of itself.
Small gaps in knowledge are easy to fill once you know where they are. That's what your error log is for.
Rest is part of the plan. A fresh brain learns faster than a tired one.
The aim is not to be fearless. It is to do the work anyway.
You are allowed to be tired and to keep going slowly. You're not allowed to call yourself behind; there's no behind, only next.
Every concept you learn now is one less surprise on exam day.
One good habit beats ten bursts of motivation. Keep the habit small and keep it daily.
If the numbers feel rusty, that's what practice is for. Rust comes off faster than you expect.
Wrong answers are tuition fees. Pay them now, in practice, and keep them out of your exam.
You're building something here: a skill, a habit and a story you'll tell in your MBA essays. Be proud of that.
Don't compare your chapter three to someone else's chapter twenty.
A score is a measurement of preparation. You can change preparation.
The version of you on exam day will thank the version of you studying tonight. Keep going.
Doubt is normal. Acting in spite of it is what makes the difference.
There's no prize for suffering. Study smart, rest well, and enjoy the small wins.
'We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.' Will Durant
'The only way to do great work is to love what you do.' Steve Jobs, Stanford commencement address, 2005
'I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.' Nelson Mandela
'A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.' Lao Tzu
'Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration.' Thomas Edison
'You miss 100 percent of the shots you don't take.' Wayne Gretzky
'Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.' Swami Vivekananda
'Dream, dream, dream. Dreams transform into thoughts and thoughts result in action.' A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
'The expert in anything was once a beginner.' Helen Hayes
'It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop.' Confucius
Think of the exam as a language you're learning. Early on you stumble over words; later you hear patterns without thinking.
If a question terrifies you today, remember it will be routine in two months. That's how learning works.
Pick one thing to be good at today: perhaps fractions, perhaps timing. One thing is enough.
You are not racing anyone. You are climbing at your own pace, and the view gets better.
Not every day has to be a great one. It just has to happen.
Your future classmates are also fighting with percentages tonight. You're in good company.
Hard work you can see: the streak, the lesson count, the question total. Look at them when you doubt yourself.
Aim for the next question, not the final score. The score takes care of itself when the questions do.
You've done harder things than a standardised test. Remember the exams, the deadlines, the campaigns. You can do this.
Make today's goal so small you cannot fail. Momentum will take care of the rest.
When Delhi traffic doesn't move, you wait and keep your mind steady. Treat plateaus the same way; they pass.
Studying at 6am or 10pm, it's all the same hours, and you are the one choosing to use them well.
Be kind to yourself like you would be to a friend preparing for a big exam. Same rules apply.
The GMAT rewards calm thinking. Calm comes from preparation, and preparation comes from the work you do today.
Mistakes show you where the points are hiding. Go find them.
Your goal is a place in a top programme. Your task today is ten good questions. Keep your eyes on today.
Let your standards be high and your self-talk be gentle. Both can be true.
Three months from now you'll know what today could not. Keep going, and let time do its part.
Winning isn't getting every question right. It's getting a little sharper every week.
Aim for steady, not spectacular. Steady is what wins this exam.

milestones.firstLesson: First lesson done, {name}. That's the hardest one, because it's the one that breaks the inertia. Everything after this is momentum.
milestones.firstPractice: Your first practice set is in the books. Don't worry about the score. You just gave the app a baseline, and now we know where to aim.
milestones.streak3: Three days in a row. That's the point where a habit stops being a plan and starts being a pattern.
milestones.streak7: A full week without missing a day. This is what steady looks like. Treat yourself to something nice, you've earned it.
milestones.streak14: Two weeks straight. Your brain is already getting used to this rhythm, which means it's getting easier to start each day.
milestones.streak30: Thirty days. A whole month of showing up for yourself. Most people quit long before this, and you didn't.
milestones.streak60: Sixty days of consistency. You're no longer someone who is trying to study for the GMAT. You are someone who studies for the GMAT.
milestones.streak100: One hundred days. That is serious discipline, and it will pay off on exam day and in every application essay you write after.
milestones.lessons10: Ten lessons finished. You now have a real foundation, and the later topics will feel less scary because of it.
milestones.lessons25: Twenty-five lessons done. You're past the halfway mark of the learning phase. Take a minute to notice how much you now know.
milestones.lessonsAll: Every lesson completed. The learning is done; now it's about sharpening. Practice, review mistakes, and trust the work you've put in.
milestones.questions100: One hundred questions answered. Each one trained your pattern recognition, even the ones you got wrong.
milestones.questions500: Five hundred questions. That's a serious body of practice. Check your error log: the patterns in your mistakes are your next big win.
milestones.questions1000: A thousand questions. You've seen most of the tricks the GMAT likes to play, and you're getting faster at spotting them.
milestones.firstMock: First full mock complete. Two hours of focus is a real achievement. Whatever the number says, it's data, not a verdict.
milestones.mockPersonalBest: A new personal best on your mocks. The work is showing. Look at what changed since the last one and keep doing it.
milestones.phaseComplete: Phase complete. Pause for a moment and celebrate, then take a look at what comes next.

comeback: Welcome back, {name}. Life happens, and nobody is keeping score. Let's start with one small session and rebuild from there.
Missed a few days? That's normal. Skip the catch-up marathon and just do today's plan, nothing extra.
Hey {name}, glad you're here. Start with ten minutes of flashcards to warm up your memory, then see how you feel.
No guilt, {name}. The GMAT rewards consistency over time, not perfection, and a short gap barely dents your progress.
A break isn't a failure. Your brain actually consolidates what you learned while you rest. Pick up where you left off.
Welcome back. Don't try to make up for lost time. Do one lesson or one practice set and call it a win.
Everyone drifts sometimes, even people with perfect schedules. The only thing that matters is that you're back.
Hi {name}. If you've forgotten some things, that's fine. A quick review is faster than relearning, so start with your flashcards.
Welcome back. Choose the easiest task on your plan and do it today. Momentum is easier to rebuild than to force.
Hey {name}. Let's reset together: today, a short session; tomorrow, the same. We'll be back on track in a week.
afterBadSession: That one stung, but it's useful. Every wrong answer shows exactly what to study next. Write it in your error log and move on.
A rough session doesn't erase your progress. Scores wobble up and down; the trend over weeks is what counts.
Take a breath, {name}. Bad sessions happen to every GMAT student. Review what went wrong tomorrow when your head is clear.
Don't judge your ability by one session. Tired, distracted or hungry brains underperform. Try again after rest.
Mistakes are cheap here and expensive on exam day, so you just got a bargain. Note what caught you out.
Hard session? Good. It means you're working at the edge of what you can do, which is exactly where learning happens.
Let's break it down: was it a concept gap, a careless slip, or a timing issue? Each has a different fix, and you can solve all three.
Step away, have some water, and come back with an easier set. Finishing on a win helps your confidence.
One bad day does not undo a month of good ones. You are still ahead of where you were last week.
It's okay to feel frustrated. Use it: pick the three questions you missed and understand them completely before the next session.

phaseIntros.foundations: This is where we rebuild your maths and reasoning basics, with no pressure and no jargon. You'll review arithmetic, fractions, percents and number sense, and start getting comfortable with how GMAT questions are put together. The goal isn't speed yet, it's understanding. Do a bit most days, take notes in your own words, and don't skip the quick checks at the end of each lesson. If something feels rusty, that's normal after years away from school maths. Spend time here, because everything later stands on it.
phaseIntros.core: Now we get to the heart of all three sections. You'll work through algebra, word problems, statistics and counting in Quant, the main Critical Reasoning and Reading Comprehension question types in Verbal, and the Data Insights formats. Each topic follows the same rhythm: learn the idea, try worked examples, then practise. Keep an error log from day one and review it weekly. Aim for accuracy first and let speed come naturally. This is the longest phase, so pace yourself and protect your rest days.
phaseIntros.advanced: You know the topics; now you make them hard. This phase mixes question types, raises the difficulty and starts adding time pressure. Expect to get more wrong, and treat that as the point, since hard questions are where scores move from good to great. Focus on your weakest areas, learn the traps the GMAT sets, and practise deciding quickly when to guess and move on. Short, sharp timed sets work better here than long, tired marathons.
phaseIntros.mocks: Time to rehearse the real thing. You'll sit full-length mock exams under exam conditions: same timing, same order of sections, no pausing. After each mock, spend as long reviewing as you did testing; the review is where the learning happens. Track your scores and your timing by section. Don't panic over one number, look at the trend. Practise your break routine and your test-day habits too, so nothing feels new on the day.
phaseIntros.taper: The heavy lifting is done. In these final days, you ease off: lighter sessions, reviewing flashcards and your error log, and maybe one or two short timed sets to stay sharp. Don't learn new topics or take a brutal mock the night before. Sleep, eat well, check your passport and exam logistics, and get your head calm. Confidence comes from the work you've already put in, so trust it.
phaseIntros.applications: The GMAT is behind you, and now the score has to do some work. This phase is about choosing schools, planning rounds, shaping your story and writing essays that sound like you. Use your GMAT score to shortlist realistically, line up recommenders early and give yourself time to rewrite. Applications reward clarity and authenticity more than polish. Take it step by step, and keep your timeline visible so nothing sneaks up on you.
